name: Cardinal Noun

dimensions.form: Cardinal numerative in noun category; may be proper or common
dimensions.meaning: Denotes number entities, quantities, labels, or numerical tokens
dimensions.function: Heads NPs in various uses (naming, quantifying, labelling)
dimensions.distribution: Subject, object, complement; proper uses are bare, common uses take determiners

1.definition: Cardinal numerative used as a noun to denote a number entity or quantity concept

constraints.description: Denotes a number entity or quantity concept, not a determiner function.
Proper-noun uses head bare NPs; common-noun uses take determiners and plural.

projection.target: A quantifying or token use can take number inflection and another determiner, as in two tens. The naming use ten in Ten is even and the determinative use in ten cards lack that count-noun environment.
projection.evidence: Reynolds separates cardinal nouns used to name, count, or label from syntactic determiner function.

curious.title: Number words that act as nouns
curious.summary: A number word can name a number, label one thing or stand for a quantity, behaving like an ordinary noun.
curious.body:
A number word can come before a noun, as in ten cards. But it can also be a noun in its own right. In Ten is even, ten names a number and doesn't count anything. In Room 101, the number labels one particular room.

Other uses count or measure. You can say a ten, and in hundreds of people the number gives a large quantity. In these uses the number word can take a plural ending and another word before it, as in two tens. The naming use and the use before a noun, as in ten cards, don't work that way.
curious.try: Compare I have ten cards with I have two tens. In which one can you put a word like two in front of the number?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why a number word sometimes behaves like a noun, with its own plural and determiner, and sometimes doesn't.
teacher.explain: A cardinal noun is a number word used as a noun. Proper-noun uses head bare noun phrases: Ten is even (the number itself) and Room 101 (a numerical label). Common-noun uses take determiners and plural forms: a ten, two tens, hundreds of people. They denote number entities, quantities, labels or numerical tokens, and they are not determiners. Contrast ten cards, where ten is a determinative and the noun is cards.
teacher.terms: Cardinal number or numeral: the traditional names. This dictionary separates the cardinal determinative (ten cards) from the cardinal noun (Ten is even, two tens).

contrasts.note: Determinative use. Ten determines the noun cards.
Common-noun use. Tens is a plural noun with its own determiner.

watch_for: A learner might read Room 101 as one hundred and one rooms.
A learner might think ten in Ten is even is counting something, when it names the number.
A learner might expect ten cards to take a determiner before ten and a plural ending, as two tens does.
teacher.activity: Give students cards with ten cards, two tens, Ten is even and Room 101. They sort them into "number before a noun" and "number used as a noun", then say how they decided.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Cardinal Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/cardinal-noun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, fa37529).
